title: Ringing in Ears After Drinking: Causes, Relief and When to Worry
excerpt: Why your ears ring after a night of drinking, from loud venues and aspirin to tonic water and the brain's rebound, how long it lasts, what helps, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Ears ringing after drinking? Why it happens (noise, aspirin, quinine, rebound), how long it lasts, what helps, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** ringing in your ears after a night of drinking is common, and most of the time it fades within a few hours to a day or two. In most cases the alcohol isn't the main culprit. The usual cause is the setting you drank in: a loud bar, a concert, a club, or a wedding with speakers next to the dance floor. Alcohol makes that worse in a few quiet ways. It dulls your sense of how loud things are, it changes blood flow and fluid balance in the body (including the inner ear), and it disrupts your sleep, which makes ringing easier to notice. Less often, the cause is something you took alongside the drinks, like a high dose of aspirin.

**The quick rules:** If the ringing is in both ears, started after a loud night, and is slowly getting quieter, it's most likely a temporary noise effect. Give your ears quiet, drink water, and sleep. If you suddenly lose hearing in one ear, if the sound pulses in time with your heartbeat, or if the ringing comes with severe dizziness, vomiting, a bad headache, or weakness in your face, get medical help quickly. Sudden hearing loss is treated as urgent because treatment works best when it starts early.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general research. It is not medical advice and does not replace an exam. **Get same-day care (urgent care, an ENT, or an emergency department) if** you notice sudden hearing loss or a "muffled" feeling in one ear that doesn't clear, ringing in only one ear along with dizziness or the room spinning, ringing with a severe headache, confusion, slurred speech, face drooping, or weakness on one side (call 911 for these), or ringing after taking more aspirin than the label allows (call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** in the US). **Book a regular appointment if** the ringing lasts more than a week or two, keeps coming back after drinking, is only ever in one ear, or pulses with your heartbeat. **If you drink heavily most days** and notice ringing along with shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or seeing or hearing things when you cut back, those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal. Talk to a doctor rather than stopping suddenly on your own, because withdrawal can become dangerous.

## What That Ringing Actually Is

The medical name for hearing a sound that has no outside source is **tinnitus**. People describe it as ringing, buzzing, hissing, whistling, humming, or a high-pitched whine. It isn't a disease on its own. It's a symptom, a sign that something in your hearing system is irritated, tired, or sending mixed signals.

Your inner ear contains a snail-shaped organ called the **cochlea**, lined with thousands of tiny sensory cells called hair cells. Each one responds to a particular pitch. When sound waves bend these cells, they send signals along the hearing nerve to your brain, which turns them into sound.

When those hair cells are overworked or stressed, for example by hours of loud music, they can misfire or go quiet for a while. Your brain's hearing centers notice the drop in normal input and turn up their own sensitivity to compensate, a bit like turning up the gain on a microphone. That extra internal "gain" is one of the leading explanations for why people hear ringing after loud noise. It's also why ringing seems louder in a quiet bedroom than on a busy street.

Alcohol touches this system at several points, which is why the question "does alcohol cause tinnitus?" doesn't have a simple yes or no answer.

## The Most Common Cause: A Loud Night, Not the Drinks

Think about where you were drinking. If it was a bar with a live band, a club, a stadium, a festival, or a party with a big speaker, the ringing is very likely a **temporary noise effect**. Audiologists call the short-term dulling of hearing after loud noise a "temporary threshold shift." You might notice that voices sound muffled, that your ears feel full, and that there's a high-pitched tone in the background. It usually fades over hours to a couple of days.

The US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) notes that sounds at or above about 85 decibels can damage hearing with long or repeated exposure. Many bars, clubs, and concerts run well above that. A single loud night usually causes temporary symptoms, but repeated nights can add up to permanent hearing loss and ringing that doesn't go away.

### Why alcohol makes loud nights worse for your ears

Alcohol doesn't make sound louder, but it changes how you behave around it and possibly how your ears cope with it:

- **You stop noticing how loud it is.** Alcohol dulls discomfort and judgment. Music that would feel painfully loud sober feels fine after a few drinks, so you stay closer to the speakers and for longer.
- **You shout to be heard.** Conversation in a loud venue means leaning in and raising your voice, and the people around you do the same, right next to your ears.
- **You skip ear protection.** Earplugs are easy to forget or dismiss once you're a few drinks in.
- **Your ear's natural protection may be weaker.** Your middle ear has a small reflex that tightens in response to loud sound and slightly dampens it. Some research suggests alcohol can slow or blunt reflexes like this, along with how the brain processes sound. The evidence here is limited, so treat it as a possibility rather than a settled fact.

The practical lesson is simple. If you notice ringing after drinking in a loud place, the sound is the thing to fix first. Foam earplugs or musician's earplugs (which lower volume evenly so music still sounds clear) are cheap, and they're the single most effective way to avoid next-day ringing.

## Ringing in Ears After Drinking in a Quiet Place

Some people get ringing even when they had a few glasses of wine at a quiet dinner. That points to effects of alcohol on the body rather than noise. Several are possible, and more than one can happen at once.

### 1. Blood flow and blood pressure changes

Alcohol widens blood vessels (vasodilation) in the short term, which is part of why your face may flush. Over the following hours, especially after several drinks, heart rate often rises and blood pressure can swing. The inner ear depends on a steady supply of blood through very small vessels, and changes in circulation are one proposed reason some people notice a whooshing or ringing sound after drinking.

If what you hear is a **rhythmic whooshing that matches your pulse**, that's called pulsatile tinnitus. After drinking, it's often linked to a faster or harder heartbeat, which you may notice more when lying down with one ear on the pillow. Our guide to [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains why that happens. Pulsatile tinnitus that continues once you're sober and rested should be checked by a doctor, because it can sometimes point to a blood vessel or blood pressure issue worth looking into.

### 2. Fluid shifts in the inner ear

The inner ear is filled with fluids that need to stay at the right volume and salt balance for hearing and balance to work properly. Alcohol affects fluid balance throughout the body. It suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally helps you hold on to water, so you urinate more. Our article on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers this in detail.

Alcohol also gets into the inner ear fluid itself. That's the well-established reason drinking causes the spins. Alcohol changes the density of the fluid and structures in the balance canals, so they send false "you're moving" signals. You can read more in our guide to the [drunk spins](/never-hungover/drunk-spins). The hearing part of the inner ear sits right next to the balance part and shares the same fluid system, so it's plausible that the same shifts contribute to a ringing or full feeling, though this is less studied than the effect on balance.

### 3. Your brain's hearing centers rebounding

Alcohol is a depressant. It boosts the brain's main calming chemical (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory one (glutamate). As alcohol wears off, the brain swings the other way for a while and becomes more excitable than usual. This rebound is behind the 3 a.m. wake-ups, jumpiness, and anxiety many people feel the next day.

The hearing system is part of the brain, so it can swing too. A more excitable auditory system may "turn up" background noise that you'd normally filter out. This is one reason tinnitus can feel **worse the morning after** than it did during the night out. In people who drink heavily on most days, this rebound can be much stronger and is part of the alcohol withdrawal picture, which needs medical attention (see the box at the top).

### 4. Poor sleep and next-day fatigue

Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it fragments sleep later in the night and cuts into REM sleep. Being tired makes tinnitus harder to ignore. Many people with long-term tinnitus report that it's louder and more bothersome when they're exhausted or stressed. If you also [can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking), the ringing and the poor sleep can feed each other.

### 5. Stress, anxiety, and paying attention to it

The day after drinking is often a day of low mood and edginess. Anxiety doesn't create ringing out of nothing, but it changes how much attention you pay to it. Once you notice a faint tone and start worrying about it, it tends to seem louder. That's not "all in your head" in a dismissive sense. It's how the brain's attention and hearing systems work together.

## Ringing in Ears After Drinking Gin and Tonic: The Quinine Question

If your ringing seems to follow gin and tonics or vodka tonics in particular, you may have heard that quinine is to blame. There's a real basis for that idea, with an important catch.

**Quinine**, the ingredient that gives tonic water its bitter taste, is a medicine that has long been used to treat malaria. At medicinal doses it's known to cause a set of side effects called **cinchonism**, and ringing in the ears is one of the classic signs. The FDA has also warned against using prescription quinine for leg cramps because of its side effects.

The catch is the dose. Tonic water contains far less quinine than a medicinal dose. In the US, the FDA limits quinine in beverages to a small amount (83 parts per million), which is a fraction of what's in a single quinine tablet. For most people, a few tonics in an evening is unlikely to cause ear ringing from quinine alone.

Still, a few situations are worth knowing about:

- **Some people are sensitive to quinine** and react to smaller amounts, including with ringing, nausea, or a rash.
- **Very large amounts** of tonic water over a long night add up.
- **Quinine interacts with some medications**, and it can be a problem for people with certain heart rhythm or blood conditions. If you take prescription medicine, ask your pharmacist whether tonic water is fine for you.

If you suspect tonic water, the simplest test is to switch mixers next time (soda water with lime works for most clear spirits) and see whether the ringing still happens. If you get hangovers mainly after gin nights, our [gin hangover guide](/never-hungover/gin-hangover) has more on why.

## Ringing in Ears After Drinking and Taking Aspirin

This is the medication link people most often miss. **Aspirin is a well-known cause of ringing in the ears**, especially at high doses. Aspirin belongs to a group of drugs called salicylates, and too much salicylate in the blood affects the cochlea. Ringing is one of the early warning signs of taking too much, and it usually goes away once the drug clears.

Here's how this tends to happen after a night out:

- Someone takes aspirin before bed or in the morning to head off a headache, then takes more a few hours later.
- They also take a combination product (some cold, flu, or "hangover" products contain aspirin or other salicylates) without realizing it.
- Alcohol plus a lack of food and water makes the stomach more vulnerable, and the person ends up uncomfortable as well as ringing.

Normal label doses of aspirin are much less likely to cause ringing in most people, though sensitivity varies. **If you develop ringing after taking more aspirin than the label allows, or after taking several products that might contain it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US)**, even if you feel otherwise fine. Aspirin and alcohol together also raise the risk of stomach bleeding. Our guide to [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) covers timing and safer choices. If you need a painkiller after drinking, read the [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) guide too, since every option has trade-offs.

Other medicines can also cause or worsen ringing, including some antibiotics, some diuretics ("water pills"), and some cancer drugs. If you take a prescription medicine and notice new ringing, mention it to your doctor or pharmacist. Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own.

## Ringing in Ears After One Drink

Getting ringing after a single drink, in a quiet place, is less common and more worth paying attention to. A few explanations are possible:

- **You already have mild tinnitus** that you usually don't notice, and the small changes in blood flow or brain activity from one drink bring it to the surface. Many people only realize they have background ringing when something makes it louder.
- **Caffeine and alcohol together.** A rum and cola, an espresso martini, or an energy drink mixer adds caffeine to the picture. Research on caffeine and tinnitus is mixed, and several studies have not found that cutting caffeine helps most people, but some individuals say it makes their ringing worse. See our guide on [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) for how the two interact.
- **An inner ear condition.** People with **Ménière's disease**, an inner ear disorder that causes episodes of vertigo, ringing, ear fullness, and fluctuating hearing, often list alcohol as one of their triggers, along with salt and caffeine. If your ringing comes with spinning dizziness and a full feeling in one ear, a doctor should rule this out.
- **Jaw clenching or neck tension.** Problems with the jaw joint (TMJ) and tight neck muscles can affect tinnitus. If you clench your teeth when you drink or sleep poorly after drinking, that can play a role.

If one drink reliably brings on ringing, it's worth booking a hearing test. That's not because something serious is likely, but because it gives you a baseline and can catch early hearing changes.

## Tinnitus Worse After Drinking: If You Already Have Ringing

Plenty of people live with long-term tinnitus and want to know whether drinking will make it worse. The honest answer is that it varies a lot between people.

Surveys of people with tinnitus have found mixed results. Some report that alcohol makes their tinnitus louder, others notice no change, and some say a drink or two makes it less bothersome in the moment, probably because alcohol relaxes them and takes their attention off the sound. Large population studies haven't given a clear, consistent answer either. Some have found moderate drinking linked to slightly lower rates of tinnitus, and others have found no link or a link with heavier drinking. These are observational studies, which can't show cause and effect.

What that means in practice:

- **Your own pattern is the best guide.** Keep a simple note for a few weeks of what you drank, where you were, how you slept, and how your ringing was the next day. Patterns usually show up fast.
- **"Feels better tonight, worse tomorrow" is a common pattern.** Alcohol may take the edge off in the moment, then the rebound, poor sleep, and next-day stress push the ringing back up.
- **Loud venues matter more than the drinks for most people.** If you have tinnitus, protecting your hearing in loud places is far more important than whether you have one glass of wine at home.
- **Heavy, long-term drinking is a different story.** Several studies have linked long-term heavy drinking with hearing loss, possibly through effects on the nerves and the brain's hearing pathways. Hearing loss and tinnitus often go together.

The American Tinnitus Association and many audiologists suggest a common-sense approach: notice your personal triggers, protect your ears from noise, manage sleep and stress, and get a hearing evaluation if tinnitus is bothering you. Sound therapy (using background noise like a fan or a sound app at night) and a form of talk therapy called CBT have reasonable evidence for making tinnitus less distressing, even when the sound itself doesn't change.

## Ringing in Ears Hangover: What It Feels Like and How Long It Lasts

Ringing is one of the less talked-about [hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms), but it often shows up alongside the usual headache, tiredness, and sensitivity to light and sound. Hangovers already make you more sensitive to noise, so even normal sounds can feel too sharp the next day.

A rough guide to timing:

| Likely cause | What it usually feels like | Typical course |
|---|---|---|
| Loud venue (temporary noise effect) | High-pitched ringing in both ears, muffled hearing, full ears | Fades over hours, usually gone within a day or two |
| Alcohol rebound and poor sleep | Faint ringing or hissing, worse in quiet rooms, alongside a hangover | Eases as the hangover passes and you catch up on sleep |
| Fast or hard heartbeat | Whooshing that matches your pulse, worse lying down | Settles as your heart rate returns to normal |
| Too much aspirin | Ringing plus nausea or feeling unwell after several doses | Needs a call to Poison Control; eases as the drug clears |
| Inner ear problem (for example, Ménière's disease) | Ringing in one ear with spinning dizziness and fullness | Comes in episodes; needs a doctor's assessment |
| Noise-induced hearing damage | Ringing that never fully goes away after loud nights | Can become permanent; needs a hearing test |

If ringing from a loud night hasn't improved at all after two or three days, or if your hearing still feels dull, see a doctor or audiologist. Persistent symptoms after noise can mean more than temporary strain.

## What to Do About Ringing in Your Ears After Drinking

There's no quick cure for ringing ears, but these steps help most people get through it and lower the odds of it happening again.

### Right now (the night of, or the next morning)

1. **Get out of the noise.** If you're still at the venue and your ears are ringing, that's a signal your ears have had enough. Step outside, take a break, or call it a night.
2. **Give your ears quiet, but not total silence.** Rest your ears from loud sound for at least a day. In bed, gentle background sound like a fan, white noise, or soft rain sounds can make the ringing less noticeable without adding strain.
3. **Drink water and eat something.** Rehydrating won't fix noise damage, but it helps with the dehydration, low blood sugar, and general hangover that make every symptom feel worse.
4. **Skip more alcohol.** A "hair of the dog" drink only delays the rebound. It doesn't fix it.
5. **Go easy on painkillers.** Avoid stacking aspirin doses, and check labels on combination products for aspirin or other salicylates. If you need pain relief, follow the label exactly.
6. **Sleep.** A proper night's sleep is one of the best things you can do for next-day ringing.

### Before your next night out

1. **Carry earplugs.** Foam earplugs cost very little. Reusable musician's earplugs cost more but lower the volume evenly so music and voices still sound natural. Put them in before your ears start ringing, not after.
2. **Stay away from the speakers.** Distance makes a big difference to how much sound reaches your ears.
3. **Take quiet breaks.** Ten minutes outside every hour or so gives your ears time to recover.
4. **Pace your drinks.** Alternating with water and eating beforehand keeps you more aware of your surroundings, including how loud things are. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) has more practical steps.
5. **Test your mixers.** If tonic nights seem to cause it, switch to soda water.
6. **Check your medicines.** Ask a pharmacist whether anything you take regularly can affect hearing or interact with alcohol.

### Things that probably won't help

You'll find a lot of supplements marketed for tinnitus online, including ginkgo, zinc, magnesium, and various "ear health" blends. Reviews of the research generally haven't found good evidence that these reduce tinnitus for most people. Some, like ginkgo, can interact with blood thinners. Ear candling is not recommended and can cause burns. If tinnitus is a real problem for you, an audiologist is a better investment than a supplement.

## Can Drinking Cause Permanent Tinnitus?

For most social drinkers, the honest answer is that the drinks themselves are unlikely to cause permanent ringing. The bigger long-term risk is **repeated loud nights**. Each time noise causes ringing and muffled hearing, the hair cells in your inner ear are under strain. They usually recover from a single episode, but they don't regrow once they're lost, and repeated episodes can add up to permanent hearing loss and long-term tinnitus. Research in animals also suggests that loud noise can damage the connections between hair cells and the hearing nerve even when hearing seems to recover, which may show up years later as trouble hearing in noisy places.

Long-term heavy drinking is a separate concern. Studies have linked it with changes in the brain's hearing pathways and with hearing loss. If you drink heavily most days and are noticing hearing changes, mention it to your doctor. It's one more reason to look at your overall drinking with a professional, not something to feel ashamed about.

The takeaway is encouraging. Ringing after a night out is usually your ears asking for a break, and you have a lot of control over the main cause. Earplugs and some distance from the speakers do more to protect your hearing than anything else on this page.

## When Ringing in the Ears Is an Emergency

Most ringing after drinking is harmless and temporary. These situations are not, and they're worth knowing by heart:

- **Sudden hearing loss in one ear**, with or without ringing. Doctors treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss as urgent, and guidelines recommend assessment as soon as possible because treatment (often steroids) works best when started early. Don't wait to "sleep it off."
- **Ringing with signs of a stroke**: face drooping, arm or leg weakness on one side, slurred speech, sudden confusion, a sudden severe headache, or loss of balance. Call 911.
- **Ringing after taking too much aspirin** or other medicine. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US).
- **Ringing after a head injury**, including a fall while drinking. Get checked, especially if you have a headache, vomiting, or drowsiness. Our guide to [severe hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/severe-hangover-symptoms) covers other warning signs that look like a hangover but aren't.
- **Ringing in one ear with spinning dizziness, vomiting, or ear pain and fever.** This needs a medical assessment.
- **Ringing as part of withdrawal.** If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, confusion, or hallucinations when you cut down, seek medical care. Withdrawal is a medical condition, and doctors can make it much safer.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that many people take around drinking. Its research focuses on how the body handles alcohol and on the brain's GABA system, which is part of the rebound effect described above. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data so far.

To be clear about the limits: **there is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats tinnitus**, and it does nothing to protect your ears from loud music. Earplugs do that. Some people take DHM because they find their general next-day symptoms easier to handle, and if that's you, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly pure DHM tablet, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. If you take prescription medicines, check with your pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Ringing in the ears after drinking is usually temporary and most often caused by **loud venues**, with alcohol making you less aware of the noise.
- In quiet settings, likely causes include blood flow changes, inner ear fluid shifts, the brain's rebound as alcohol wears off, and poor sleep.
- **Aspirin** is a well-known cause of ringing at high doses. Tonic water's quinine is a much smaller factor for most people, though some are sensitive.
- If you already have tinnitus, your response to alcohol is personal. Track your own pattern and protect your ears in loud places.
- **Sudden hearing loss in one ear, stroke signs, possible overdose, or withdrawal symptoms need prompt medical care.** Ringing that lasts more than a week or two deserves a hearing check.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do my ears ring after drinking?**

Most often because you were drinking somewhere loud, like a bar, club, or concert. Loud sound temporarily strains the hair cells in your inner ear, and alcohol makes you less aware of how loud it is. In quiet settings, ringing can come from changes in blood flow, shifts in inner ear fluid, the brain's rebound as alcohol wears off, poor sleep, or high doses of aspirin taken for a headache.

**How long does ringing in the ears last after drinking?**

Ringing after a loud night usually fades within a few hours to a day or two. Ringing linked to a hangover tends to ease as the hangover passes and you sleep. If it hasn't improved after two or three days, your hearing still feels muffled, or it keeps coming back, see a doctor or audiologist for a hearing check.

**Does alcohol cause tinnitus?**

Alcohol can contribute to temporary ringing, but for most social drinkers it isn't the main cause. Loud venues are the bigger factor. Research on alcohol and long-term tinnitus is mixed: some people find drinking makes their tinnitus worse, others notice no change. Long-term heavy drinking has been linked with hearing loss in several studies.

**Can tonic water cause ringing in the ears?**

Quinine, the bitter ingredient in tonic water, can cause ringing at medicinal doses. Tonic water contains much less quinine than a medicinal dose, since the FDA caps it at 83 parts per million in drinks, so a few tonics are unlikely to cause ringing for most people. Some people are more sensitive to it. If you suspect it, switch to soda water and see if the ringing stops.

**Can aspirin after drinking make my ears ring?**

Yes. Aspirin is a well-known cause of ringing in the ears, especially at high doses, and ringing is an early warning sign of taking too much. Avoid stacking doses and check combination products for hidden aspirin. If you get ringing after taking more than the label allows, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the US. Aspirin and alcohol together also raise the risk of stomach bleeding.

**Why are my ears ringing after just one drink?**

One drink can bring background tinnitus you didn't notice to the surface through small changes in blood flow and brain activity. Caffeinated mixers, jaw clenching, and inner ear conditions such as Ménière's disease can also play a part. If one drink reliably causes ringing, or it comes with dizziness or a full feeling in one ear, get a hearing test.

**Why is my tinnitus worse the day after drinking?**

As alcohol wears off, the brain becomes more excitable than usual for a while, and that can turn up the background noise your hearing system normally filters out. Fragmented sleep and next-day stress make ringing harder to ignore. That's why some people find a drink takes the edge off in the moment but leaves their tinnitus louder the next morning.

**When is ringing in the ears after drinking an emergency?**

Get urgent care for sudden hearing loss in one ear, since treatment works best when it starts early. Call 911 for ringing with face drooping, one-sided weakness, slurred speech, confusion, or a sudden severe headache. Call Poison Control if you may have taken too much aspirin. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, or a racing heart when you cut back, see a doctor about withdrawal.

**Does DHM help with ringing in the ears?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats tinnitus, and it doesn't protect your ears from loud music. Earplugs and distance from speakers do that. DHM's research focuses on alcohol metabolism and the brain's GABA system, mostly in animal studies. Some people take it for general next-day symptoms.
